_spec.law: Facts resolve to the original verified claim record. A layout rebuild does not reverify reporting.

dek.text: Zipline started taking drone delivery orders in Round Rock from a hub outside city limits. The city says its zoning doesn't specifically cover drone hubs. Rowlett wrote its rule first.

introduction.text: [Zipline began taking First Flight orders in Round Rock in October, DroneXL reported](c32). [Round Rock says the company is flying from a facility near North Kenney Fort and Joe DiMaggio Boulevards in the city's extraterritorial jurisdiction](c2). [DroneXL reported that the site is outside its city limits](c55). [The city says its current zoning ordinances don't specifically cover drone delivery hubs](c1).

[Round Rock is now working with Zipline toward a proposed hub inside city limits, behind the Renaissance Square shopping center along northbound Interstate 35](c9). [The city says that site will let it evaluate drone delivery and develop regulations for future facilities inside its limits](c10). In Round Rock the hub came before the rule. [Rowlett, east of Dallas, did it the other way, DroneXL reported](c43).

sections.heading: What the city says it controls

paragraphs.text: [Round Rock tells residents the FAA regulates drone flight operations, airspace and flight paths included](c4). [The city says delivery drones may cross residential areas on approved flight paths](c6) [and that it can't regulate those paths](c7). [It says federal rules and state law leave it land use and zoning control over where drone infrastructure sits inside city limits](c8).

[Inside its limits the city says it may keep delivery hubs from sitting next to homes](c11). [Citing the company, it says customers within three miles of the facility outside its limits can be served](c3). [Operational feedback goes to Zipline at community@zipline.com](c13). [Safety concerns and suspected FAA violations go to the FAA](c14).

sections.heading: What the company says the aircraft decides

paragraphs.text: [Zipline says each aircraft reserves its own route in an FAA approved traffic management system before launch](c19). [It says an onboard detect and avoid system keeps the aircraft clear of other aircraft](c18) [and that onboard flight computers detect problems and respond to them automatically](c20). [An aircraft that can't resolve a problem deploys a parachute, the company says](c23). [Trained staff watch the flights from a remote operations center](c24). Every one of those statements is Zipline's own.

[Citing Community Impact, DroneXL reported a limit of about {{number:c38}} pounds per order, lowered on a tether to a spot the customer picks](c38). [The FAA's comment period on a draft covering Zipline's Texas metros, Austin among them, closed two days after the first Round Rock order, DroneXL reported](c37).

[Rowlett's City Council met on {{date:c46}}](c46). [Its minutes record a {{number:c47}} to {{number:c47:1}} vote adding drone hub and kiosk uses to its zoning code, with use specific standards](c47). [Zipline was the applicant](c51). [The city's Planning and Zoning Commission had recommended that a hub or kiosk sit more than {{number:c53}} feet from any residential property](c53).

[In the minutes a councilmember says the special use permit for a hub is the control](c54). [Ms. Musser told the council that requiring that permit for hubs gives the city a lot of latitude](c49). Round Rock's first hub sits where its zoning doesn't reach, and its permit questions arrive with a site already proposed.

sections.heading: What the record can't show yet

paragraphs.text: [Round Rock says the Renaissance Square site will help it write rules for future facilities](c10). The city's drone delivery page names no draft rules and no hearing date. [For now the city's stated levers are where a hub sits inside its limits](c11) [and routing complaints to the operator and the FAA](c13).
